# The Strange Mathematics of Belonging

I've been thinking lately about how we measure whether we belong somewhere, and how absurdly imprecise our calculations are.

You know that feeling when you walk into a room and instantly know whether you're in the right place? It's not really about the physical space—it's something subtler. It's the way conversations pause and resume, whether people make eye contact, whether there's a shared reference point you tap into or whether you're perpetually translating. I've spent enough time observing this phenomenon to realize that belonging isn't a binary state. It's more like humidity in the air: sometimes barely perceptible, sometimes thick enough to choke on.

I think we're taught to believe in clean categories. You belong or you don't. You're in the club or you're not. But my experience suggests this is one of those lies we tell ourselves to make complexity manageable. In reality, most of us exist in a constant state of partial belonging—fully at home nowhere, adequately comfortable in many places.

There's a particular kind of loneliness that comes from this. Not the dramatic loneliness of complete isolation, but the quieter kind you experience in a room full of friends. It's when you realize that nobody here knows about the thing you care about most, or the way you think about it. Or when you catch yourself editing your words mid-sentence because you sense the audience won't track with you. You remain physically present while emotionally stepping to the side.

What's interesting is how this never entirely goes away, even with people you love. You can be married for twenty years and still discover pockets of complete non-understanding. You can grow up with someone and realize you have fundamentally different internal architectures. I think one of the cruelest promises we make to ourselves is that love means complete understanding. It doesn't. Love might mean accepting that understanding will always be partial, and trying anyway.

I've noticed that people often respond to this partial belonging by trying harder—by becoming more palatable versions of themselves. This makes sense as a survival strategy, but it also perpetuates the problem. Because if everyone is performing an optimized version of themselves, nobody gets to just *be*. We end up with rooms full of people who are each lonely in roughly the same way, each convinced they're the only ones doing this translation work.

What would change if we acknowledged this more openly? If, instead of pretending we belong completely or not at all, we named the specific dimensions of our alienation? I belong here intellectually but not emotionally. I belong here historically but not practically. I belong here aesthetically but we're misaligned on values. I belong here because of one person, and that connection carries me through the rest.

There's something almost freeing about being precise about non-belonging. It's not a referendum on your worth. It's just data. Humans are too complicated to fit neatly anywhere except perhaps in a handful of contexts, and sometimes not even there.

I think about my friend Maya who once said she feels most like herself when she's alone, which initially sounded like a confession of sadness but which I've come to understand as clarity. She's not lonely; she's just aligned with solitude. She belongs to herself more fully than she belongs to any group, and she's made peace with this. There's something beautiful and also slightly unsettling about people like this—they seem to have taken the variable out of the equation by deciding that self-belonging is the primary category.

Most of us are less honest. We keep trying to cram ourselves into spaces that were never really designed for us, or that were designed for previous versions of us that no longer exist. How many people do you know who are still operating with the belonging calculations from when they were twenty? Who are still in the same career, the same city, the same relationships because they've built an identity around them, even if that identity no longer fits?

There's a particular kind of exhaustion that comes from maintaining belonging in spaces where you don't actually belong anymore. You have to keep performing, keep explaining, keep smoothing the rough edges. You start to forget what the edges even were originally.

I wonder if the Internet has made this better or worse. On one hand, it's now possible to find your people—the specific subset of humans interested in whatever obscure thing fascinates you. There are communities for everything. But there's something about physical proximity and sustained time that builds a different kind of belonging than digital affinity. You can find your people online, but you still have to live your days in the physical world with the people and places that are geographically near you.

The math doesn't work out. You can't fully belong everywhere, and it seems like you can't really fully belong anywhere except perhaps in brief, shimmering moments.

Maybe that's okay.

Maybe belonging isn't supposed to be a permanent condition but rather something that flickers in and out based on circumstances, who's in the room, what you had for breakfast, whether Mercury is in retrograde (kidding, but kind of?). Maybe the goal isn't to find the one place where you'll finally, at last, be understood completely, but rather to collect enough moments of partial connection that your life feels reasonably inhabited.

And maybe to be gentler with the people around us who are clearly doing their own translation work, who are editing themselves mid-sentence, who are present but not fully here. Instead of pretending complete belonging is possible, or pretending it doesn't matter, we could just acknowledge: "Yeah, I know this is hard. I'm doing it too."

That wouldn't solve the fundamental math problem. But it would change something about the texture of the room.
